text: Extensibility is an architecture goal, not a deferred goal.
Primitives/adapters/hooks are designed for the full matrix of stores/buckets/streams/transports from the start.
Only implementing the long tail is de-prioritized.
"Plumbing not a matrix" was implementation priority, not an architecture limit.
Both tier-1 editions are fully featured.
Store work proceeds redb → +Turso/SQLite/IndexedDB.
That work is built to accommodate future backends without redesign.
Postgres is a plausible future backend.
NATS-stream is a plausible future message transport.
Kafka is supportable, not Drew's choice.
Custom connection types per operation type are supportable.
An extension system exists: callbacks/hooks along all normal paths.
New protocols/backends are adapter code against stable primitives.
(implied) No core logic hard-codes a single store/bucket/stream/transport.
(implied) Adding a backend is additive, not a breaking refactor.
(implied) Parity is defined at the primitive layer; a backend limitation is a conformance gap, not a product tier.
(implied) Hooks are part of the normal execution-path contract, not a debug afterthought.
Every peer belongs to an explicit peer class; no unclassed peer.
Class: fully trusted.
Class: send-only (we send, we do not accept).
Class: accept-signed-from.
(implied) Classification is directional, not symmetric.
(implied) Classification is per-peer, not global.
(implied) Class governs acceptance behaviour; it does not by itself confer cryptographic trust.
(implied) Class is changeable over time (promote/demote/revoke) without redesign.
(implied) Default class for an unknown peer is the most restrictive: no acceptance.
(implied) Send-only is a legitimate permanent posture, not a degraded state.
(implied) Fully trusted does NOT mean exempt from validation.
Data is accepted ONLY when cryptographically signed AND validated — every source, no exceptions by source.
Unsigned data is not accepted, even from a fully trusted peer.
Invalidly signed data is not accepted, even from a fully trusted peer.
(implied) Internal peers are under the same gate as external.
(implied) Local/loopback/in-process channels are under the same gate — no channel exception.
(implied) Validation is distinct from signature presence (a non-verifying or misattributed signature fails).
(implied) Validation binds data to a signer identity, not merely to "some valid signature".
(implied) Acceptance is a gate at ingest, not post-hoc cleanup.
(implied) The gate is a mechanism/invariant, not a behaviour configuration may switch off (tension with §7 — ruled in principle 3).
(implied) Key rotation must not retroactively invalidate data validly signed under a then-current key.
(implied) Key revocation/compromise has a defined effect on previously accepted data (revalidate/flag/quarantine).
(implied) Replay/freshness protection is required: re-presented old signed data is handled by a specified rule.
(implied) Signature-suite agility: deprecating an algorithm must not break the protocol.
(implied) Rejection under the gate is an observable, recordable event (silent drops would defeat reputation and inconsistency detection).
Internal peers carry implicit trust — a posture distinct from external federation peers.
Implicit-trust peers sync toward 1:1 sameness.
Sameness is qualified "within reason" — a convergence target, not an absolute invariant.
(implied) "Within reason" includes storage capacity, retention policy, configured scope.
(implied) "Within reason" includes tenant/trust-domain boundaries — sameness never crosses a boundary data must not cross (see #9083).
(implied) Sync is convergence over time; temporary divergence is normal.
(implied) Divergence is detectable (otherwise "sync toward" is unverifiable).
(implied) Anti-entropy/reconciliation is the implied mechanism class; specifics deferred to the CRDT exploration.
A sync conflict's first output is a conflict report.
Reports come before any automatic merge — no silent auto-resolution precedes the report.
(implied) A conflict report is a first-class artifact (addressable, retainable, actionable), not a log line.
(implied) A report identifies the conflicting versions, signers/sources, and the data in dispute.
(implied) Unresolved conflicts do not block unrelated sync.
CRDT/merge exploration is explicitly later — a research track, not a dependency of the first federation design.
(implied) Conflict-report-first remains available even if a merge mechanism is later adopted.
Research: evaluate **Automerge** (data-model fit, fleet-scale performance, signed-history compatibility, interop cost).
Research: identify what "diamonds" refers to (believed Diamond Types) and evaluate on the same criteria — the identification is part of the research.
Research: evaluate the **Willow protocol** (reconciliation efficiency, namespace/subspace model vs our scoping, signed-only acceptance fit).
Research: evaluate **OCAPN** (capability authority model vs the peer-class model; can attenuation express send-only / accept-signed-from natively?).
(implied) The four explorations are a named set evaluated on a common criteria matrix.
(implied) The set is not exhaustive — other prior art found is captured, not excluded.
A federated query checks the server's own store first.
Then it fans out to remotes.
Fan-out targets a prioritized list of remotes.
Those remotes are known not to hold everything.
(implied) A remote's negative answer is not a global negative.
(implied) Prioritization is explicit, by stated criteria.
(implied) Prioritization inputs (trust class, reputation, coverage, latency, cost) are design decisions, candidates for configuration.
A trusted remote may re-fan-out to its remotes — recursion.
(implied) Re-fan-out is restricted to trusted remotes; relay authority is not granted to accept-only peers.
Recursion is bounded by max-hops.
(implied) Max-hops is a stated bound carried by every query (decremented/tracked per relay).
Signatures and validation apply throughout: query, relayed copies, responses.
(implied) A relayed response preserves the original responder's signature end-to-end — no hop-by-hop authority substitution.
(implied) Relayed responses are validated to the direct-response standard.
(implied) Fan-out must not amplify without bound; breadth × depth is a resource surface max-hops alone doesn't bound.
(implied) A query carries a stable request identity across all copies/relays (prerequisite for duplicate handling).
(implied) Fan-out leaks query interest to every remote queried — a named privacy surface, accepted or mitigated explicitly.
The same request can legitimately arrive more than once (direct + via relay) — normal, not an error.
All four duplicate behaviours are specced: inform users, short-circuit, dedup, loop-inform.
Inform: a duplicate is surfaced to the requester, not silently swallowed.
Short-circuit: a duplicate of an in-flight/answered request is not re-executed from scratch.
Dedup: duplicate work/results are deduplicated into one coherent result set.
Loop-inform: duplication evidencing a loop is reported specifically as a loop.
(implied) Duplicate-vs-loop discrimination needs request identity + hop/path information.
(implied) Dedup is by request identity, not query text — the same query asked later is a new request.
(implied) Dedup state is finite; its retention window and expiry behaviour are specified.
Servers may store routing state.
Servers periodically validate their known network shape against reality.
(implied) Routing state goes stale; staleness is expected and handled.
(implied) Validation detects at least vanished peers, appeared peers, topology changes affecting fan-out.
(implied) Routing state is an attack surface (poisoning redirects fan-out, suppresses results, manufactures loops) — routing updates fall under the same signature/validation discipline as data.
(implied) A server's known shape is partial by design; no complete topology is assumed.
A reputation system exists: peers carry ratings.
(implied) Ratings derive from evidence, not assertion alone.
(implied) Reputation feeds behaviour — at minimum fan-out prioritization and peer-class changes.
Trust adapts from evidence automatically per stated rules (not only manual reclassification).
Takeover case (explicit): a highly trusted server turns malicious (takeover or key compromise); the system must survive it.
(implied) Trust must be revocable at speed — slow adaptation is not a defence.
(implied) Blast-radius limit: data accepted from a taken-over server before detection is identifiable as a set.
(implied) A defined post-detection posture for that server's prior data (revalidate/flag/quarantine/repudiate) is chosen and specced.
(implied) Takeover vs honest key compromise are distinguished, or explicitly conflated — recovery differs.
Reputation includes protections against bad actors abusing the reputation system itself.
(implied) Protections cover rating manipulation: ballot-stuffing/self-promotion, retaliatory down-rating, Sybil raters — a stated position per failure mode.
(implied) Protections cover whitewashing (fresh identity resetting reputation) — in tension with open federation, recorded as a tension.
(implied) Protections cover collusion — load-bearing, because collusion is the defeat condition of inconsistency detection and cannot be assumed away.
A public log for claims and disputes about federation conduct exists.
Entry form: "server X claims Y was done incorrectly" — a claim by an identified server about another's act.
(implied) Entries are claims, not verdicts.
(implied) The accused party can answer in the same log (right of reply).
(implied) Entries are attributable and non-repudiable — signed by the claimant.
(implied) The log is append-only in effect; corrections are new entries.
(implied) The log is evidence input to reputation.
(implied) Frivolous/spam claims are themselves a bad-actor case needing protection (no cost-free smear/flood channel).
Inconsistency is detectable from acknowledgments: what a server acknowledged receiving is evidence against its later claims.
Worked example (explicit): A says "don't have it"; B produces a recipient list including A — contradiction.
(implied) Detection is by a third party comparing denial vs recipient list; it does not require A's cooperation.
(implied) Acks/recipient lists are retained and producible as evidence.
(implied) Acks are signed/non-repudiable to serve as evidence.
Defeating detection requires collusion (e.g. B withholds/falsifies the recipient list).
(implied) Collusion is the residual, accepted-by-analysis risk — detection raises the cost of lying from one server to a colluding set; it does not make lying impossible.
(implied) The size/composition of the colluding set needed is a security parameter worth stating.
(implied) A detected contradiction belongs in the public log and in reputation evidence.
Threat case: tampering with (federated) search results is a named threat.
(implied) Tampering decomposes into omission, injection, reordering/manipulation, staleness.
(implied) Injection is bounded by the signature gate (an injected result can't carry its claimed source's valid signature) — omission is the hard case, leaving no cryptographic trace.
(implied) Omission detection depends on cross-checking and acknowledgments — the design states which countermeasures it uses.
(implied) A remote claiming completeness for a scope can be caught omitting; whether remotes make completeness claims is a recorded design decision.
Our system is not special.
Every capability is a configuration option anyone could replicate; none is reserved to our implementation by the protocol.
(implied) No privileged protocol position for our servers (same classes, reputation, log exposure).
(implied) No hardcoded self-preference (no default trust/priority exemption for our nodes that a replicator couldn't also configure).
(implied) Non-specialness is testable as interop: an equivalently configured independent implementation participates equivalently.
(implied) First-party/hosted deployments are instances of configurations, not a distinct kind of system (link: #9078).
(implied) We cannot be the unaccountable operator/arbiter of the reputation or log systems — that would be a special position.
The system has different modes.
Different kinds of links exist.
Different kinds of storages exist.
(implied) A mode is a named, selectable posture — not a code fork.
(implied) Link kinds are distinct from peer classes but interact (sync link, query/fan-out link, send-only link; usable link kinds follow from peer class).
(implied) Storage kinds differ in federation-relevant properties (durability, retention, whether the storage participates in sync/fan-out at all).
Tiering may be built directly in.
(implied) Tiering may apply at several layers (storage, data, trust/peer, query-priority) — the design says which.
(implied) Built-in tiering lives in the core model: records carry their tier natively.
Behaviours are expressed as configuration where what varies is behaviour.
…and as primitives where what varies is mechanism.

(implied) That rule is a classification test applied to every federation/trust feature (peer classes, max-hops, prioritization, sync scope, mode = configuration; signature validation, acknowledgment, dedup identity, fan-out recursion = primitives).
(implied) Configuration cannot override a primitive's invariant — no config disables signature validation (resolves S1.20).
(implied) Modes are bundles of configuration: selecting a mode sets many behaviour values coherently; individual values remain overridable.
(implied) Modes compose with per-peer configuration — mode is deployment posture, peer class is per-relationship posture; neither collapses into the other.
(implied) Mode/link/storage selections are themselves replicable configuration under non-specialness (S1.115).
Benchmark latency/characteristics: D1 vs R2 vs laptop redb vs laptop Turso.
Benchmarks run at various shard levels.
Benchmarks run as DBs grow — size is a dimension, not a fixed fixture.
A tenant hot cache exists in D1.
Hot-cache admission is by tenant tier / compute usage.
Recent heavy/frequent queries skip the Turso hop via the hot cache.
Tenant stores possibly live IN D1.
Alternative: tenant stores are SQLite files synced to S3/R2 on an interval.
Existing tooling for SQLite-file sync is evaluated before building new.
One, or a set of, R2/RustFS buckets serves many ID instances.
Shared buckets have a trusted mode: sync just ID + hash.
Shared buckets have an untrusted mode: broker and/or encryption.
In untrusted mode, co-tenants see only encrypted blobs.
Garbage collection is designed for this storage model.
GC prioritizes very large files.
(implied) Benchmarks report economics as well as latency (cost per tenant / per query shape, per shard level and size).
(implied) Hot-cache invalidation/staleness vs the Turso source of truth is specified; skipping the hop is valid only within a defined freshness bound.
(implied) Trusted vs untrusted is a per-bucket/per-tenant threat model, not a global flag.
(implied) GC for large files avoids re-upload/rewrite of a whole file to reclaim a small fraction — chunk/segment reclamation matters.
Much/all ID-ingested content is auto-queued for vectorization.
Vectorization uses Snowflake + the second embedder from Atlas #9092.
Built-in ID search is a platform feature, not an add-on.
Recommendations are "news feed" / "you might be interested" surfaces.
ONE worker fans out for recommendations.
A Durable Object accumulates recommendations incrementally.
The consumer API is incremental: "give me the next 10".
Recommendations are stored as their own objects.
Search history is stored (as recommendation objects/inputs).
Stored recommendations enable admin before/after comparisons.
Some recommendation data has shorter retention.
"What's hot" intermediate data is the example short-retention class.
(implied) Ingest → vectorize is asynchronous/queued, not blocking ingest.
(implied) Both embedders' outputs are searchable/comparable; embedder choice is not hard-coded.
(implied) Incremental accumulation survives restarts — hence a Durable Object, not in-memory paging.
(implied) Retention is per data class, not one global TTL.
(implied) Before/after comparison requires versioned/timestamped recommendation snapshots.
Multiple ID shapes are supported; no single canonical format.
(implied) Consumers dispatch behaviour by ID shape.
(implied) New shapes can be added without invalidating existing IDs.
The content-addressed hash is one supported shape.
A hash ID needs no map (no lookup table/registry/translation layer).
Store hash, ship hash — the stored hash is transmitted unchanged.
(implied) A hash ID is portable across servers, buckets, transports without re-issuance.
(implied) A hash ID is verifiable by recomputation over the content.
(implied) Identical content yields the same hash ID (natural dedup).
(implied) A hash ID names content independently of where copies live.
Metadata lives in a sidecar beside the hash, not inside the hashed content.
(implied) Keeping metadata outside keeps the hash stable when metadata changes.
The default sidecar form is a file/object named `hash.metadata`.
`hash.metadata` contains ALL metadata for that hash (complete, not a subset).
Alternative A: one R2 path/filename per metadata version.
Alternative B: the sidecar is a pointer to `hash.metadata.<date>`.
(implied) S3.13–S3.16 are undecided alternatives, not three simultaneous mandates.
(implied) The dated form makes each metadata version an immutable, addressable snapshot.
(implied) The pointer form is a mutable "latest" indirection over immutable dated versions.
(implied) The R2-path form needs defined escaping/encoding for hashes, versions, dates in paths.
The metadata may contain related path links.
(implied) Related links are path references, not restricted to hash IDs.
A server receiving a hash can acknowledge its existence.
(implied) Existence acknowledgement is a distinct operation from returning content or metadata.
(implied) Existence ack enables replica/inventory checks without content transfer.
A harvesting process collects sidecar metadata and inserts location records into a location index.
Harvesting can run as a batch process.
Harvesting can run immediately on receipt/ingest — a deployment choice, not a format difference.
The harvester inserts ALL location records found, not only a primary one.
Location records include an R2 bucket location.
Location records include a laptop location as hostname + path.
Location records include a Drive location prefixed by account (no cross-account collisions).
Location records include a Drive URL.
The location-type list is open-ended ("etc.") — new types expected.
(implied) One hash has many concurrent location records of different types.
(implied) The sidecar is the harvester's source; the location index is derived and rebuildable.
The location index ties directly to Atlas VFS #9100.
(implied) Deletion/move/stale-location handling for harvested records is unspecified and must be designed.
A namespace is a named addressing space with its own rules, distinct from its host server.
A server hosts multiple namespaces.
Each server has a namespace registry.
The registry is definable per server.
Different servers' registries may diverge — by design.
(implied) No global namespace registry and no globally canonical resolution exists.
(implied) The same name may resolve differently on different servers without either being in error.
Each namespace can have its own URL handler.
Each namespace can have its own encoding (e.g. base64).
(implied) Encoding is per-namespace, not a global URL property.
An `id://` URL design covers these namespaces.
It must follow the URI specifications.
It must be human-readable.
It must be expandable without breaking existing URLs.
Drew's `idb64+...` sketch is NOT adopted — it is a sketch to evaluate/replace.
(implied) Human-readability rules out a common case that is only an opaque base64 blob.
(implied) URI compliance constrains scheme, authority/path, reserved characters, percent-encoding, case/normalisation, length — all to be settled in the design.
(implied) A namespace definition declares at least: core type, handler, encoding, resolution/write rules.
Exactly two core namespaces exist, from which families derive.
Core (a) is the content-addressed namespace.
Core (b) is the array-address namespace.
(implied) Derived families are configurations/compositions of a core, not new storage primitives, unless a design proves otherwise.
In core (b), an address is an array of byte-strings.
Each array item is either null or bytes.
(implied) Item order is significant — position is part of the address.
Address length is arbitrary, 0..n.
The zero-length address is valid.
(implied) Null items are meaningful sparse slots, not merely absent values.
A bare string query is shorthand for an array address.
A bare string resolves via a server-configurable default index.
Drew's example configuration is index 2 with [0],[1] null.
S4.31 is one server's configuration, NOT the rule — never hardcoded.
(implied) Different default-index configs resolve the same bare string to different addresses.
Values are stored as TYPE + BYTES (type tag + payload).
Equality is type-sensitive: number 1 ≠ string "1".
(implied) Identical bytes with different type tags are different values.
Serialization is type-aware.
(implied) Serialization round-trips: a value reads back with the type it was written with.
Arbitrary objects serialize into this namespace.
(implied) The object serialization format, and which types are primitive vs encoded objects, must be designed.
Interfaces may stream results.
Interfaces accept a max-items parameter.
(implied) Streaming + max-items require defined truncation/continuation semantics.
(implied) Max-items is an interface capability, not a limit on address length or stored items.
A derived string-path namespace of human, Wikipedia-style names exists.
Example: `us president.md` (spaces, extension included).
A name resolves to a target, per-server.
Resolution may be hand-picked by the admin.
Resolution may be picked algorithmically.
(implied) Both modes must be representable per server.
(implied) Names are expected to be ambiguous/colliding; multiple candidate resolutions exist.
Search shows the resolutions (plural), not a hidden winner.
Resolutions are lens-able.
Lens 1: own server's overrides.
Lens 2: popularity by total count.
Lens 3: popularity among users you have interacted with.
Lens 4: popularity among users of a given standing.
(implied) "Standing" must be defined (what it is, who assigns it, how it's queried).
Authority groups curate names/resolutions.
A group is adoptable as a preferred filter/lens.
Example: a "wiki group" curating Wikipedia-style names.
(implied) Adopting a group is voluntary — a preference, not a global authority.
(implied) Multiple groups can curate overlapping names; a viewer can switch preferred group.
A derived numeric-registry family exists (addresses/values are numbers).
Integers supported.
Floats supported.
Decimals supported.
Bigints supported.
Numbers are infinitely growable (no fixed max magnitude/precision).
(implied) That requires an extensible byte encoding, not fixed-width fields.
A numeric registry may be the byte system plus numeric-style write validation.
(implied) Numeric-ness is then enforced at write by validation, not a separate engine.
(implied) Validation defines canonical encoding, ordering, precision, and rejection rules per numeric kind.
A derived stream namespace family exists.
Text streams.
Chat-as-typed in multi-user documents (contributions addressable while produced).
Voice in progress.
Video in progress.
(implied) A stream is addressable before it finishes; in-progress state is first-class.
A finished stream redirects to the final stored object.
(implied) The redirect is namespace semantics: following a completed stream's address yields the stored object.
(implied) Stream lifecycle and write-vs-subscribe rights must be designed.
A namespace definition can be signed by an authority.
Drew signing a definition is the canonical example.
A signed definition designates the world data its coordinates land in.
Coordinates are tuple addresses in the world (e.g. ID 1,3,7).
(implied) Coordinate worlds are naturally expressed on the array-address core.
Resolving a coordinate lands in the signer-designated world data.
World content is presentable/renderable, not only raw fetch.
A signed world is read-only for others.
Others remain free to serve whatever they want on their servers.
(implied) A signature confers canonicity for that signer's world, not a protocol monopoly.
(implied) Signature verification, signer key identity, and revocation/re-signing must be designed.
Everything breaks down into triples.
Infinitely many triples are allowed.
Storage is NOT pretty-printed UTF-8 JSON.
Investigate compressed/streamable binary encoding.
Investigate JSONB.
Investigate normalized byte-key→byte-value maps.
Graph storage must be efficient at scale.
Graph query languages are evaluated/supported.
Graph visualization is in scope.
Metadata is accessed via the graph when graph query lands.
(implied) Triple encoding preserves streaming/partial read; no whole-graph load to answer a query.
(implied) Visualization consumes the same graph query layer, not a separate store.
"User attributes" is Drew's term, distinct from Atlas metadata.
…and distinct from content-location metadata.
User attributes = metadata on a user's user object.
Attributes are themselves objects.
Example: the `name` attribute of the `geordi.png` path.
Example: comments at `geordi.png/comments`.
Attributes can be append-list attributes.
Anyone may SUBMIT a signed comment object + hash for append.
The server appends in server-defined central order.
Submitters cannot set/edit the list directly.
The owner/group admins control the object generally.
An explicitly OPENED attribute accepts append submissions despite that control.
Non-group submitters go to a PENDING queue.
Pending submissions need member/admin approval per configuration.
(implied) Append order is authoritative only from the server.
(implied) Signature + hash are verified before append or queueing.
(implied) Opened vs closed is an explicit per-attribute state.
Infinitely nesting objects are the substrate for social apps.
Feeds/Twitter-like apps are buildable.
Profiles/Facebook-LinkedIn-like apps are buildable.
Bulletin boards (phpBB/Usenet/Reddit/HN-like) are buildable.
Accepted objects become topics.
Comments on comments are supported.
Comment objects are content-addressed in the mutable area.
Forum views carry a cheap freshness TOKEN.
Token semantics: latest check / since-date / before-date.
(implied) The token proves "nothing new" without a full scan/refetch.
(implied) Nesting depth is not capped by the data model; caps are view/policy.
Mutable-area items are editable by owner/admins.
Versioning is a `succeeds` triple, v1 → v2.
Views show v2 by default.
Views carry v1 comments forward onto v2.
Carried comments are asterisked as old-version comments.
TRUE DELETE is governed by server policy.
Server admins can true-delete.
GC can true-delete when an item is unreferenced.
Group admins/users can mark their own items for next-batch deletion.
Marking is batched, not immediate.
A firehose "please delete / please moderate" queue exists for admin review.
(implied) Marking, moderation-queueing, and true deletion are three distinct states.
(implied) A referenced object is not GC-deleted even if marked, until references clear or policy overrides.
Assigning array[0..1] = [null, user's public ID (iroh key)] makes a space client-validatable as that signer's.
Petname attributes exist, distinct from canonical IDs.
Delegations: other keys can own/write a location.
Delegation is expressed via a well-known location listing delegations/transfers.
Alternative: identity triples ("XYZ is the same as 123").
An identity triple is accepted only when CROSS-SIGNED.
Cross-signed = both sides state/publish toward each other.
The exact delegation/cross-signing ceremony must be designed.
(implied) Client validation must not require trusting the server for signer identity.
(implied) A unilateral identity claim is at most pending/unverified, not a delegation.
(implied) Transfer (replaces owner) and delegation (grants, may not revoke the original) are distinct.
